Judicial questions include retention of 12th Judicial District judges, including Stephen P. Ochoa and Angie K. Schneider, a special election for Division 2, and magistrate races. Retention is a yes-or-no vote, not a contest between candidates.

Statewide questions include four constitutional amendments and three general-obligation bonds. The amendments cover the governor’s pocket veto, school-election timing, a salary for legislators tied to median household income, and university regent appointments. The bonds are for senior facilities (about $21.6 million), libraries (about $19.3 million), and higher-education, special-school, and tribal-school projects (about $352.2 million), repaid with a statewide property-tax levy. Otero County also has a local bond question on the ballot.

What to bring

New Mexico does not require photo identification for most voters. First-time voters who registered by mail and did not provide ID then may be asked for identification. Anyone unsure of status, precinct, or ballot should look up the record at nmvote.org or call the clerk before Tuesday.

item.title: IPRA Task Force Issues Recommendations to the Legislature
item.description:
ALAMOGORDO — The state task force charged with reviewing New Mexico’s Inspection of Public Records Act has sent lawmakers 11 recommendations, including an out-of-state fee for police body-camera review, a new ombudsman, and factors courts would weigh before imposing the law’s daily penalties. Open-government members on the panel voted against the pieces most likely to change how the public enforces the statute.

The letter went Thursday to the interim Courts, Corrections and Justice Committee and the Legislative Finance Committee. It is not the final report. The task force said that report, with majority and minority positions and the public comments it received, is due by Oct. 15. House Joint Memorial 2, sponsored by Rep. Cathrynn N. Brown and co-sponsored by Sen. Natalie Figueroa and Rep. Matthew McQueen, directed the New Mexico Department of Justice to convene the panel and report on IPRA’s “workability and effectiveness.”

The Santa Fe New Mexican reported Friday that the letter appeared on the Department of Justice website that morning and that references to it were gone by 5:30 p.m. The task-force page still describes the panel and its listening tour, including the June 22 stop in Alamogordo.

The eight-member panel held 11 public meetings — Clovis, Roswell, Carlsbad, Alamogordo, Las Cruces, Silver City, Gallup, Farmington, Las Vegas, Santa Fe, and Albuquerque — and took 312 comments in person and online. It then held seven deliberative meetings. Members are Madeleine Zaritsky of the Department of Justice, who chaired the panel; Rebecca Martinez of the New Mexico Municipal League; Michael Eshleman of the New Mexico Association of Counties, a former Otero County attorney; Belinda Mills of the New Mexico Press Association; Lalita Moskowitz of the ACLU of New Mexico; Kenneth Stalter, a plaintiff’s attorney; Ethan Watson, a defense attorney; and Greg Williams of the New Mexico Foundation for Open Government.

What drew opposition

The sharpest split is on fees, penalties, and a new office that would sit between requestors and court.

Six members favored a statutory scheme requiring out-of-state requestors to pay the actual cost of reviewing and redacting body-camera footage. Any residency rule, the letter says, should account for victims, people who are indigent or unhoused, legitimate newsgathering, and other out-of-state requestors with a real interest in New Mexico records. Fees collected would have to be dedicated to IPRA staffing, technology, training, and redaction. Moskowitz opposed it. Eshleman abstained.

Six members favored an IPRA ombudsman, or similar office, that would train both sides, run a hotline, issue non-binding advisory opinions, mediate, and collect compliance data for the Legislature. Moskowitz and Williams opposed that recommendation. An advisory office that does not bind agencies can become a delay if custodians treat it as a substitute for the deadlines and damages already in the statute.

Five members favored a non-exclusive list of factors for courts deciding statutory per-diem penalties under Section 14-2-11 and whether a denial was unreasonable. Moskowitz and Williams opposed it. Mills abstained. IPRA’s daily penalty is the main consequence when a custodian misses a deadline or withholds a record without a lawful exemption. A factor list written for agencies can narrow that remedy without an explicit repeal.

What passed with less friction

Three recommendations were unanimous: more money to digitize paper records, including large-format building plans; proactive publication of record classes that do not need redaction, plus a public portal for a person’s own traffic-crash report; and a duty for a requestor to answer a custodian’s good-faith fee demand within a set time or have the request closed.

Seven members backed standardized statewide reporting of IPRA data, possibly with a volume threshold. Martinez opposed it. Seven backed more training tied to custodians’ needs and the Department of Justice training budget. Walker Boyd, sitting as Eshleman’s proxy, opposed it. Seven backed a credentialing program in public records, through a state agency or a New Mexico university. Zaritsky abstained. Seven backed grants so public bodies can buy request-management and redaction software. Stalter did not vote.

Seven members also backed a coordinated review of the Children’s Code, victims’ rights statutes, and IPRA confidentiality rules, with attention to whether protections follow a record when it moves to law enforcement, a district attorney, or another public body. The letter says any change should not create exemptions broad enough to block oversight. Moskowitz opposed it.

Why it matters here

Alamogordo Town News has used IPRA and the Open Meetings Act to obtain city and county records on hiring, budgets, ethics complaints, and closed-door commission business. Those requests are in-state newsgathering, not commercial harvesting of body-camera video. The letter’s own caveat for “legitimate newsgathering” is the line the 2027 session will have to write in statute if the body-camera fee moves forward. A fee that local outlets can waive on paper and still cannot pay in practice is a barrier.

The Department of Justice page frames the review around request volume that has more than doubled since 2020, commercial data brokers, and out-of-state and out-of-country filers. Open-government groups on the panel have argued that volume is not a reason to weaken the right of New Mexicans to inspect the records their governments already hold.

The full report, including rejected ideas and the comment appendices, is scheduled for the same two committees by Oct. 15. Nothing in the letter is law. Each item still needs a bill, a hearing, and a vote in the 2027 session.

item.title: Analysis: Nagamine Draws Clear Lines on Data Centers While Block Lets His News Site Speak
item.description:
Summary

Nagamine: a concrete policy stance. A data center proposal must have closed-loop water, a noise mitigation plan and its own power with no effect on the grid or on local residents, or it would not be considered.

Block: no position in his own name was found. The news site he founded and edits has welcomed the state’s largest data center project and criticized those who would pause the industry, which amounts to a tacit endorsement.

 Endorsement: the Sierra Club Rio Grande Chapter confirmed its endorsement of Nagamine on Aug. 29.

 Caveat: Block’s stance is inferred from what his site publishes, not from a statement or a vote.

ALAMOGORDO — On data centers, the two candidates for House District 51 have given voters very different amounts to go on. Independent Grace Nagamine has laid out specific conditions a project must meet or not be considered. She also carries the endorsement of the Sierra Club Rio Grande Chapter into the Nov. 3 election.

State Rep. John Block, R-Alamogordo, has not taken a position in his own name, as far as a search for this article found. The Piñon Post, the conservative news site he founded and edits, has done the talking. It has welcomed the industry’s largest New Mexico project and gone after the politicians who want to slow it.

Nagamine’s stand

Nagamine has said a data center proposal must meet three conditions or it would not be considered:

• A noise mitigation plan

• Self-sustaining power, separate from the grid, with no effect on electric rates for neighboring communities, small businesses or residents

• Closed-loop water use that does not draw on local aquifers or on areas already short of water

The position is conditional, not a ban. It stops short of the statewide moratorium that Democratic gubernatorial nominee Deb Haaland and some Doña Ana County legislators have proposed.

It fits the rest of her campaign. Her published platform calls water the district’s most urgent fight and pledges to pursue state funding for Alamogordo’s water and sewer rebuild.

In a September video reported by Alamogordo Town News, she listed high electric prices among the issues she said the race should be about.

The Sierra Club endorsement

The Sierra Club Rio Grande Chapter confirmed its endorsement of Nagamine in an Aug. 29 email from Richard Barish, the chapter’s political chair. The email followed a phone call and said she was free to announce it at any time.

Barish thanked her for “stepping up to run for the legislature” and for her commitment to the district’s residents. He said the chapter would list its endorsements in the October-December issue of its quarterly newsletter.

The chapter’s own position on the issue is public. In a Sept. 17 statement, it said it supports a moratorium on data centers until enforceable guardrails are in place, citing climate pollution, water and electric bills.

Nagamine’s conditions address the same concerns, water and electric rates among them, without calling for a moratorium.

Block and the Piñon Post

The site’s author page identifies Block as its founder and editor. Its data center articles carry a “Piñon Post” staff byline however he is owner and editor responsible for all content decisions. 

A June 23 article on Project Jupiter, the Oracle and OpenAI campus in Doña Ana County, said the project could become “a major win for southern New Mexico” if it delivers on its promises. It answered water concerns with Oracle’s figure of about 11 million gallons of non-potable water in closed-loop systems. It acknowledged drought, said New Mexico should grow, and called for transparency and long-term protections trusting the sponsoring company statements without challenge.

Since mid-September the site has focused on Haaland. A Sept. 27 article set her moratorium pledge against at least $117,200 in contributions it tied to Oracle and industry executives. The same article said there is no evidence the money changed her positions.

Searchlight New Mexico reported that Oracle and BorderPlex also gave a little more than $51,000 to Republicans, including $10,000 each to Rep. Nicole Chavez and Sen. Larry Scott.

Block has spoken about the race, if not about data centers. In a fundraising email reported by the Santa Fe New Mexican, he said his opponent is backed by a deep-pocketed, far-left political action committee however she is an Independent and has reported support from both sides of the isle including an endorsement from former Republican Mayor of Alamogordo, Susan Payne. 

How this comparison was made for this article.

The two candidates are measured here on different kinds of evidence, and readers should weigh them differently.

Nagamine’s position comes from her own stated conditions and her published platform.

Block’s comes from what the site he edits has chosen to publish. That is an editorial record on a property he uses to attack his political opponents and is well known as his mouthpiece.

On that evidence, the difference is one of starting point. The Piñon Post owned by John Block begins from growth and treats water and power as questions to settle along the way.

Nagamine would require her conditions to be met before a project is considered.

The two overlap in places. The June article cited on-site fuel cells and closed-loop, non-potable water, features that resemble two of Nagamine’s conditions. It did not address noise or neighbors’ electric rates.

The question is not yet local. Project Jupiter is in Santa Teresa, outside House District 51. Otero County has no approved large data center, though commissioners directed staff in March to explore the idea, Alamogordo Town News reported.

Conclusion

Nagamine has given voters a concrete policy stance. A data center proposal would need closed-loop water, a noise mitigation plan and its own power, with no effect on the grid and no cost to local residents. Without those, it would not be considered.

Block has not matched that in his own name. He has left the question unaddressed while the site he controls presents Project Jupiter as an economic opportunity and aims its criticism at those who would pause the industry. Taken together, that amounts to a tacit endorsement by John Block of data centers, delivered through his publication instead of his office.

That conclusion rests on inference, and Block can settle it. He could say how he would vote on a statewide pause and what conditions, if any, he would require of a data center in Otero County.

Nagamine has lead with a concrete policy stance where is the leadership from John Block?

item.title: In Memory of Carol Lynn Hamilton
item.description:
Carol Lynn Hamilton passed away September 25, at 9:58 PM. She was born on April 28, 1944 in Pasadena, Texas to Rodney S. and Jean L. Larrabee.

Carol is survived by her husband, Spencer Hamilton, of 60 years of marriage; daughter, Teri Scott and her husband, Tim Scott, and their daughter, Jordon and son, Cole; daughter, Amy Hamilton; and son, Tom Hamilton, and his wife, Melissa Morin, and their son, Princeton.

Carol grew up in Seabrook, Texas, located on Clear Lake Shores next to NASA Headquarters south of Houston, Texas. She graduated from Clear Lake High School in League City, Texas class of '63. She got a degree as a CPA at Tarleton College at Stephenville, Texas. She and Spencer Hamilton were married on October 22, 1966, in Dawson, Texas by her friend, Reverend Love and marriage license sighed by Mark Twain. Carol and Spencer settle in Jasper, Texas where she drove a school bus for 20 plus years at Jasper School District. She won first place in a school bus driving contest in the South East Texas district and went to State in Austin, Texas and took third place.

She started a successful dog grooming and kennel business called "Hamilton's" on January 1, 1991 with her beloved daughter, Amy. She wrote an article, "Amy's Special Touch" published in Horizons magazine in March/April 1992.

Carol and her family settled in La Luz, New Mexico to be close to her grandkids.

Carol loved gardening. In her own words, "Dragonflies are on every continent except Antarctica. My connection to Dragonflies is that I have been on every continent except Antarctica" referencing worldwide travel with her family.

Services will be held at Scenic Chapel, 1334 N Scenic Drive, Alamogordo, NM on Wednesday, October 7. Visitation service will begin at 9:30 am with the funeral service at 10:30 am followed by burial at Monte Vista Cemetery.

item.title: The Minority Excuse: Measuring Rep. John Block Against His Own Caucus
item.description:
Twenty-five of 26 House Republicans had a bill signed into law in 2026. Block’s pass rate ranks 19th of 26, in the bottom 10 of his caucus. He led none of the bills that carry his name into law, and every proposal of his own failed.

ALAMOGORDO N.M. — When Rep. John Block’s thin legislative record comes up, the answer from his defenders is always the same. He is a Republican in a Democratic Legislature. The minority cannot pass bills. Judge him on something else.

So judge him against Republicans. We pulled the 2026 session record of every one of the 26 Republicans in the New Mexico House, the people who sit in the same minority, face the same committee chairs and answer to the same governor. Measured against them (fellow Republicans), Block is in the bottom third in effectiveness.

Block put his name on 37 bills, memorials and resolutions in 2026. Four passed but none that he actually sponsored to begin with. That is a success rate of 10.8%, and it ranks 19th in a caucus of 26. Only seven Republicans did worse. The caucus median is 13.8%. The average is 16.3%.

The members at the top are not household names with safe majorities behind them. Republican Rep. Jack Chatfield passed 42.9% of what he sponsored. Republicans; Rep. William Hall passed 33.3%. Rep. Brian Baca, 31.3%. Rep. Tanya Mirabal Moya, 27.3%. Rep. Catherine Cullen, a first-term member, 20.8%. Minority Leader Gail Armstrong passed seven of 40.

The bottom 10, in order, are Reps. Stefani Lord, Rebecca Dow, John Block, Alan Martinez, Jimmy Mason, Elaine Sena Cortez, Luis Terrazas, Rodney Montoya, Randall Pettigrew and Martin Zamora.

Cut the numbers another way and the picture holds. By the share of his measures that became law, Block is 18th. Among the 21 Republicans who sponsored at least 15 measures, he is 15th. Twenty-five of the 26 had a bill signed by the governor, so the minority can plainly pass legislation. First-term Republican Rep. Nicole Chavez had five.

A bill changes the law. A memorial is a statement of the Legislature’s wishes and changes nothing. A sponsor is anyone who signs on; the first-listed sponsor is the legislator who brought the bill and carried it.

Three bills that became law in 2026 have Block’s name on them. He was the first-listed sponsor on none. The medical malpractice overhaul was led by a Democrat, Rep. Christine Chandler, and by Armstrong; 49 legislators signed it, including 23 of the 26 House Republicans. The police battery bill was Rep. Andrea Reeb’s. The water project bill lists Democratic Rep. Kathleen Cates first and Block second, and came out of an interim committee. His one successful memorial, asking for a film industry task force, was a Democrat’s.

Everything Block brought on his own failed. Thirty-three measures, among them permitless carry of firearms, voter identification, chemical castration as a parole condition, a new tax on renewable energy production and year-round daylight saving time. Several were repeats of bills that failed in 2023. Most never got out of their first committee.

One of his measures passed the full House before dying in the Senate. Chavez had 13 reach that stage. Sena Cortez had nine. Armstrong, Cullen and Rep. Jenifer Jones had eight each. Those are bills that Democratic chairs agreed to hear and Democratic members agreed to vote for. That takes relationships.

Block’s campaign postcard tells voters he “delivered more than $11 million for Alamogordo and Otero County priorities.”

Here is how that money works. Each year the House divides its share of capital outlay evenly. Each member turns in a list of projects, the lists are folded into one bill, and the bill passes or fails as a package. A legislative finance handout put the 2025 share at $2.5 million for every representative. The Legislative Council Service chart for 2026 shows seven projects under Block’s name totaling exactly $2.5 million, the same figure it shows for Armstrong and Baca. The money on the postcard is the standard share, added up over four years.

Then look at how he voted on the packages. In 2023 he voted no on House Bill 505. In 2025 he voted no on House Bill 450, and no on the state budget. In 2026 he voted no on Senate Bill 240 and no on the capital outlay reauthorization bill. He picked the projects, voted against the bills that paid for them, and mailed voters a card taking credit.

In the final week of the 2026 session he was also recorded absent on four bills, including wheelchair insurance coverage and the Child Care Assistance Program Act.

Block came to Santa Fe as the publisher of the Piñon Post, a site that, as the Santa Fe New Mexican has reported, routinely labels Democrats “far-left.” Before he held office he filed a campaign finance complaint against the governor over hair and makeup expenses; the Secretary of State’s Office found no violation. In November 2024 the secretary of state told a legislative committee she had been harassed online, and her office named Block as the member she meant. Block denied it and called the accusation a publicity stunt.

No record can prove that those fights are why his bills die. That is a conclusion after speaking with members of both parties that work along side him. 

But the contrast in the data is hard to miss. The Republicans who passed bills in 2026 attached themselves to work that could win Democratic votes: licensing compacts to bring health care workers into the state, parole and pension fixes, property tax relief for disabled veterans. 

Block spent his session on bills with no path, in a building where the people he has spent years attacking decide what gets a hearing.

Four years in, his record is 174 measures sponsored and 11 signed bills carrying his name. Being in the minority explains why Republican bills are hard to pass. It does not explain why 18 other Republicans passed a larger share of theirs.

District 51 voters have a choice this year, that by Block's Party's own admission has become "a race of a lifetime." Unlike Block, Grace Nagamine is  a lifelong Alamogordo resident running as an independent, and claims to be beholden to the constituents not the party ideology of either party and  is on the Nov. 3 ballot against Block.

Where Block offers a mailer, Nagamine has published detailed position statements and draft legislation at graceforhd51.org, so voters can read what she would file before they vote. Where Block has built a brand on picking fights with the people who run the Capitol, she has committed to building collaborations with members of both parties. As an independent she owes neither caucus a vote.

The case for that approach is in the numbers above. Collaboration is how dollars and support reach rural New Mexico communities. The capital outlay packages, the water project authorizations and the licensing compacts all moved because legislators of both parties put their names on the same bill and then voted for it. Alamogordo has $160 million in water and sewer repairs ahead of it and will need every state dollar it can get.

One candidate has spent four years showing how he does the job, the numbers say ineffectively. The other is telling voters, in writing, how she would do it differently. Early voting begins Oct. 6.

A measure is credited to every member listed as a sponsor in any position. “Passed” covers bills signed by the governor and memorials or resolutions adopted without a signature.
